The official briefed news outlets by phone in the wake of numerous major disruptions at large corporations and federal agencies in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop, a protracted Microsoft Outlook outage and a reported blackout of the National Security Agency's classified communications network. Read more CNBC politics and policy coverage Jensen Huang slated to appear before House panels Dec. 1; Nvidia lawyer due to testify Dec. 2 Republicans outspent Democrats in record 2026 midterm ad blitz Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed governor won't attend Trump committee's hearing Other incidents include software issues at JPMorgan Chase , an outage at United Airlines that caused some flight delays and product issues at Apple . On Tuesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC that the outages are not a cyberattack and "not a coordinated effort by a nation state." He gave a similar assurance on Wednesday to the House Homeland Security Committee. "We have no indication that these incidents are related, that they're coordinated," Clayton said. "We also have no indication that they're result of a state-sponsored malign actor." But the sheer volume of incidents in the past week alone has raised alarm bells among consumers and tech experts alike, with some wondering if rapidly advancing artificial intelligence models are to blame. The senior Trump administration official, asked on Wednesday's call to what degree AI was involved in the outages, said it is "challenging to answer that question across all of these incidents that have been reported." Sen. Mark Warner , D-Va., vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, told CNBC Wednesday morning he wants "better coordination" on AI safety. "I understand why people are freaked out," Warner said. "The one way we could lose this AI race and [see] all of these companies' valuations plummet dramatically is if we have an AI tool run amok, or an AI-sponsored cyberattack that creates harm." His comments came hours before before Anthropic is scheduled to price its initial public offering for the first major AI industry IPO. Warner advocated for a "pre-testing regime" for new AI models that establishes guardrails and helps ensure a "culture of safety built in" to the industry." He said the U.S. is "lucky" that it has so far avoided a major AI-generated cyberattack or a crisis with a rogue agent that goes beyond incidents like Hugging Face breach earlier this year. — CNBC's Samantha Subin contributed to this report. headlines.article_text: Ford starts U.S. battery cell production using Chinese tech Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Ford has started U.S. production and shipments of battery cells for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL. The plant has been contentious for the automaker, which has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, for its connections to CATL. Ford said licensed CATL technology and manufacturing support are helping it bring lower-cost LFP cell production to the U.S. quicker. In this article F Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT An employee does final inspection before cells are put in shipping containers to be moved to Ford's battery pack plant that's connected to the cell manufacturing facility. Courtesy Ford MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL. The automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck , which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors. The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China. The automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL. Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible. "If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells." The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. US President Donald Trump (L) shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province on November 18, 2026. Lori Sagisawa | AFP | Getty Images In September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing. Ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production. Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the company's energy storage business. That's down from initial plans of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry. watch now VIDEO 3:12 03:12 Inside the facility developing Ford's EV tech Autos Ford has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed. The facility is highly automated, but Ford said it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it plans to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027. headlines.summary: Anthropic stock is set to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT on Thursday.
headlines.article_text: Anthropic IPO: AI lab considers increasing offering, sources say Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Anthropic is considering upsizing its initial public offering, according to people familiar with the details. The AI lab is expected to set its final IPO price after market close Wednesday. The stock is set to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT on Thursday. In this article ANT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei speaks during INBOUND 2025 Powered by HubSpot at Moscone Center in San Francisco, Sept. 4, 2025. Chance Yeh | Getty Images Anthropic is considering upsizing its initial public offering, people familiar with the details told CNBC, as the artificial intelligence lab weighs setting the price well above $80. The company closed its order books and locked in total demand on Tuesday, setting the stage for the Claude creator's eagerly awaited Nasdaq listing. Institutional demand for the offering is around $400 billion, while retail demand is approaching $100 billion, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. The orders are indications of interest and are not binding. All of the details are subject to change, and Anthropic will make final decisions Wednesday afternoon, the people said. Anthropic is expected to set its final IPO price after market close Wednesday. Demand for the offering is higher than it was for Elon Musk's SpaceX , even though the rocket maker had a bigger market offering. SpaceX debuted on the Nasdaq in June in by far the biggest IPO on record, ultimately raising $85.7 billion. The AI lab said last week that it would offer 825 million shares in the IPO at a price range of between $70 and $78 per share, which would net up to $64.35 billion at the high end of that range. A representative for Anthropic declined to comment. Anthropic's listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has experienced a set of recent shocks, including a dramatic backlash that was felt at the polls in the midterm elections and last week's ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The market was already jittery on concerns that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds. Tech's biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, as an investor, partner or customer. Amazon and Google both own stakes valued at over $100 billion, and a group of tech companies, including Google, Microsoft , Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices agreed to collectively invest $26 billion in the IPO. Anthropic, meanwhile, is a buyer of costly systems from Nvidia, Google, Amazon and AMD. Read more CNBC tech news Anthropic likely to price IPO above the current range of $70 to $78, sources tell CNBC Demis Hassabis’ AI company raises $5 billion, months after he left as Google DeepMind CEO OpenAI inks agreements with four independent evaluators to boost company’s safety work How Rockstar’s ‘GTA VI’ release could reshape gaming, streaming and even paid time off "I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in Anthropic's roadshow video . "We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time." Amodei co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers less than six years ago, after the group collectively defected from OpenAI. The company is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses. Anthropic has been racing to maintain an edge over OpenAI and Google in the enterprise market, and it experienced a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code. OpenAI has confidentially filed for an IPO and has said a debut is likely in 2027. For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said, it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus. The company reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said. Anthropic said in an amended filing that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month. The company has faced plenty of challenges during its meteoric rise over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, leading to two high-profile disputes with the U.S. government this year. Its prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of its IPO. "Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles," Anthropic's co-founders wrote in the company's prospectus. "Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort." Gary Hershorn | Corbis News | Getty Images A series of tech outages has consumers stocking up on emergency supplies. Costco sales are seeing a lift because of it, according to research firm Mizuho. In the final week of October, Mizuho estimates, Costco's U.S. comparable sales, excluding gasoline, rose 11% to 12%, up from the normal 6% to 7% the first three weeks in October. Costco reported an 8.1% increase for the month. The firm said the stronger pace is continuing through November, as 21 of the 26 high-ticket generators it tracked on Costco's website sold out as of Sunday night. Shares of Costco were roughly flat-to-lower in Wednesday morning trading at around $1,107 apiece. "Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at COST," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger said in a research note Monday. Bellinger will appear on CNBC's "The Exchange" during the 1 p.m. hour. On Thursday, an outage occurred in Microsoft's Outlook and Teams, and on Friday the Federal Aviation Administration halted departures nationwide. On Monday, a software outage at JPMorgan Chase caused banking transaction delays, and a system outage delayed United Airlines flights. The National Security Agency said Tuesday that the spy agency's communication network went down temporarily. The outages appear to come amid a rush to recover software vulnerabilities uncovered by AI tools, and officials are saying there's no reason for panic. Still, on TikTok and other social media platforms, posts urging people to stock up on food and supplies are gaining significant traction. Mizuho raised its price target on Costco to $1,150 from $1,100 and kept its buy-equivalent outperform rating. The firm said U.S. comparable sales could grow more than 10% in November. Mizuho also sees Walmart 's Sam's Club benefiting from emergency preparedness sales as shoppers fill up their pantries, and for Home Depot and Lowe's as they buy home improvement emergency supplies. At Costco, Mizuho will be watching whether the surge brought in new member sign-ups when the warehouse retailer reports its first quarter of fiscal 2027 on Dec. 10. headlines.article_text: Stocks moving the most today: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Workers shade themselves with umbrellas outside Nvidia's headquarters, Nov. 12, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. Take-Two Interactive also got a boost ahead of the release of "Grand Theft Auto VI", while Lowe's shares pulled back following the company posting third-quarter results. Follow along as CNBC covers the biggest stock market moves of the day. 1 Hour Ago JPMorgan upgrades Millicom stock to overweight Shares of Millicom International Cellular are up nearly 1% after JPMorgan upgraded the digital telecommunications and media company to overweight from neutral on Wednesday, maintaining a $105 price target, implying a 28% gain above Tuesday’s close of $82. Millicom International Cellular - stock price for one year JPMorgan analyst Marcelo Santos sees a buying opportunity on the stock's recent weakness. "Part of the weakness may have been due to technical factors, such as Tigo's removal from MSCI Sweden, and part due to the acquisition of Entel Peru, which we do not believe destroys value," Santos said. The upgrade comes as Millicom expands in Latin America. The company agreed last week to buy Entel's Peru business for $1.71 billion, adding to its regional footprint. — Deena Zaidi 2 Hours Ago Nvidia pop fizzles Nvidia's post-earnings gains were short-lived, with the stock last down 0.4%. If the stock falls again, it would mark its fifth consecutive daily pullback. NVDA 5-day chart — Fred Imbert 2 Hours Ago New York Times Company shares fall Shares of the legacy news media company slid nearly 3% after Citi on Wednesday downgraded the stock to neutral from buy. Analyst Jason Bazinet said near-term trends in app downloads, active users, engagement frequency and time spend are all eroding. He lowered his price target to $76, from $85, which implies roughly 3% upside from Tuesday's close for the stock. "These trends suggest New York Times may face lower sub growth due to lower conversion, lower retention, or higher churn," he wrote. Shares were higher by more than 1% in premarket trading. "We view Schwab as a clear beneficiary from higher-for-longer interest rates which should drive continued healthy net interest margin expansion," Raymond James analyst Patrick O'Shaughnessy said in a note Wednesday. "Beyond macro tailwinds, Schwab's account and net new asset growth rates are healthy and prove the company's value proposition with self-directed retail investors and RIAs remains strong. The company is also enjoying robust success with key growth initiatives such as pledged asset line lending." — Tanaya Macheel 3 Hours Ago Neoclouds rebound following Nvidia’s quarterly beat Shares of neocloud companies bounced in extended trading on the back of Nvidia's quarterly report. headlines.summary: Lowe's said it saw strength in online sales during its quarter that contributed to a guidance raise for the full year.
headlines.article_text: Lowe's (LOW) Q3 2026 earnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Lowe's said it saw strength in online sales during its quarter that contributed to a guidance raise for the full year. The home improvement retailer said it's also seeing strength among its professional shoppers. The company said it received roughly $250 million in tariff benefits during the quarter. In this article LOW Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:58 06:58 Lowe’s posts strong online sales, raises outlook despite slow housing market Squawk Box Lowe's on Wednesday posted strong quarterly results and raised its full-year outlook as the company said it saw strength among professional shoppers. The company said comparable sales grew 1.8% for the fiscal third quarter, driven by a 17.4% increase in online sales and "solid" performance in pro and home services sales. Net sales rose to $22.76 billion. Because of the strength, Lowe's now said it expects full-year sales of roughly $92.5 billion, up from a previous projection of $92 billion. It also expects comparable sales to be up 0.5%, compared with previous guidance of flat. CEO Marvin Ellison told CNBC that the company is focused on growing despite economic headwinds and a sluggish housing market. He said Lowe's posted its sixth straight quarterly comparable sales increase and saw particular strength in appliances, which saw its largest revenue growth in five years. "We believe irrespective of the macro environment we're in, we're going to take share because there's a lot of share out there that we can go and get, and we're going to be aggressive to go and get that share," Ellison told CNBC. Lowe's also reported a pretax benefit of approximately $250 million from tariff refunds during the quarter, which contributed a 34-cent boost to earnings per share. Ellison said the company plans to use those funds to enhance the customer experience and bring value to shoppers. He added that do-it-yourself customers and pro shoppers are not investing in major renovation projects but are instead spending on repair and maintenance projects. "We are giving those pros what they need," he said. "We're able to improve our fulfillment capabilities and our pro loyalty program." Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $3.10 adjusted, it was not immediately clear if that compared to the $2.88 expected Revenue: $22.76 billion vs. $22.41 billion expected For the quarter ended Oct. 30, Lowe's reported net income of $1.67 billion, or $2.98 per share, compared with $1.62 billion, or $2.88 per share, the year prior. The home improvement retailer has previously said it's seeing "pressure" on spending on projects, especially as consumers are stretched thin by inflation and macroeconomic uncertainty. The company is also battling a slower housing market and higher mortgage rates. Ellison previously told CNBC he expects consumers to remain cautious through the end of the year. Lowe's executives said on a call with analysts Wednesday that the company is continuing to battle high fuel costs, which they said accelerated through the third quarter. CFO Brandon Sink said diesel prices are currently around $6 per gallon, up about 15% overall compared to what the company saw in the second quarter. "So we're trying to continue to manage that, balance that, and we're reflecting that into our Q4 guide," Sink said. Ellison told CNBC the company remains optimistic about consumer spending this holiday season and that November sales are in line with expectations so far. Lowe's competitor Home Depot said earlier this week that it's seeing resilience among professional shoppers and reported comparable sales growth.
